title: Matt Damon's ship from 'The Odyssey' needs your help
summary:
The lifesize wooden ship that took a beating during Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is due for some much-deserved care, and its owners are looking for volunteers to help. The 50-oar Draken Harald Hårfagre is scheduled for routine maintenance, and volunteers are encouraged to apply online, provided they can get to Norway by April 2027. 'A project like Draken depends not only on a professional crew and sailing deckhands, but also on dedicated volunteers who help support the life of the ship,' reads its official website. Volunteering offers a hands-on way to contribute while learning about the vessel and the community that keeps the project moving, the website says.

Nolan's blockbuster adaptation of The Odyssey is a massive movie, and much of its scale comes from practical effects. Instead of relying on computer-generated imagery, the award-winning director used full-sized set pieces like an actual Trojan Horse. But one of the film's most prominent examples was not actually built for the movie: for the role of Odysseus' galley ship, Nolan enlisted the Draken. The Draken is not technically period-accurate for The Odyssey's Late Bronze Age setting, but neither is the movie's contemporary English dialogue, or its choice of Matt Damon as Odysseus.

Commissioned in 2010 by Norwegian oil and gas magnate Sigurd Aase, the Draken is built with overlapping oak planks based on ship descriptions in Viking skaldic poems. At 114 feet long and 26 feet wide, with a single 79-foot-tall mast, the ship is a scaled-up version of the famous Gokstad ship built around 890 CE. The Draken's maiden voyage took place in 2012, and a crew of 100 rowers successfully recreated the Vikings' transatlantic crossing from Norway to Newfoundland only four years later. Today, it routinely sails to ports around the world for exhibitions and educational tours.
why_it_matters: The Draken is a working piece of living history that teaches people about Viking seafaring, and keeping it sailing shows how real ships and practical effects can bring a story to life better than computer imagery alone.

background_read: The Draken Harald Hårfagre is a large wooden Viking-style ship built with overlapping oak planks, based on descriptions in old Viking poems.
It was used in Christopher Nolan's film The Odyssey as the ship of Odysseus, because the director preferred full-sized real sets over computer-made images.
The ship is kept going by a professional crew and volunteers, and it now needs routine maintenance, so its owners are asking for volunteers who can travel to Norway.
When it is not filming, the Draken sails to ports around the world for exhibitions and educational tours, letting people see a Viking-style ship up close.
